title: Does Depression Phenotype Predict Antidepressant Response? A Transdiagnostic Review of Phenotype-Specific Antidepressant Efficacy
content: Major depressive disorder is one of the most prevalent and disabling conditions worldwide, yet fewer than one-third of patients achieve remission with the first antidepressant prescribed. The clinical phenotypes codified across successive editions of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) — melancholic, atypical, anxious, and psychotic forms of depression — were proposed, in part, because they were thought to predict differential response to specific drug classes. This narrative review evaluates the evidence for phenotype-specific antidepressant efficacy across the full depressive spectrum, including treatment-resistant depression as a longitudinal phenotype and the transdiagnostic reformulations advanced by the Research Domain Criteria initiative. Historical controlled trials demonstrated genuine but circumscribed phenotype–drug interactions, most notably the preferential response of atypical depression to monoamine oxidase inhibitors relative to tricyclic antidepressants. However, contemporary large-scale effectiveness data from the Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to Relieve Depression (STAR*D) and the International Study to Predict Optimized Treatment in Depression (iSPOT-D) trials do not support subtype-based antidepressant selection. Much of the apparent predictive value of melancholic status is confounded by illness severity and placebo responsiveness, while data-driven re-analyses have failed to biologically validate the DSM-defined subtypes. Anxious depression and treatment-resistant depression robustly identify poorer outcomes but do not yet point clinicians toward specific drug classes. Weighing the totality of evidence, categorical depression phenotypes have limited utility in predicting antidepressant response; the most clinically reproducible signal is severity-dependent drug–placebo separation, and the most promising route to precision prescribing lies in transdiagnostic, multimodal biosignatures and machine-learning approaches.
